title: Writing with Claude
description: Use Claude as a writing partner to draft emails, essays, reports, and creative content of all kinds.

data.text: Claude is widely considered one of the best AI assistants for writing. It produces nuanced, well-structured prose that reads naturally. But the key to great writing with Claude is not just asking it to 'write something' — it is treating Claude like a skilled writing partner who needs direction, feedback, and iteration.

data.title: A practical writing workflow with Claude:
items: Define the piece: purpose, audience, length, and format
Ask Claude for an outline first — review and refine before writing
Request the full draft section by section
Ask Claude to revise based on your feedback
Proofread and edit the final output yourself

data.text: Types of Content Claude Excels At

cards.title: Professional Writing
cards.description: Emails, reports, proposals, and business documents that need to sound polished and credible.

cards.title: Long-Form Content
cards.description: Essays, articles, blog posts, and documentation that require sustained coherence.

cards.title: Creative Writing
cards.description: Stories, scripts, marketing copy, and creative content with personality.

data.text: The most important part of any writing prompt is the audience and purpose. Claude writes very differently depending on who it thinks it is writing for. Always specify the reader. Also specify the format — email, essay, social media post, report — because each has different conventions.

data.title: Effective writing prompt
data.content: Prompt: 'Write a 400-word email to our engineering team announcing that we are adopting Claude for documentation. The tone should be enthusiastic but practical — we want to get people excited without overselling. Mention that the team will get a training session next week. End with an invitation to try it on a current doc and share feedback.'

data.text: Rarely will Claude's first draft be perfect. The real power comes from iteration. After receiving a draft, give specific feedback: 'Make the second paragraph shorter', 'Add a concrete example after the third sentence', 'Change the tone to be more formal'. Claude remembers the conversation context, so each revision builds on the previous version.

data.title: The outline-first approach
data.text: Before asking for a full draft, ask Claude for an outline. Review the structure, ask for changes, and only then request the full text. This prevents you from having to rewrite large sections later and ensures the piece flows logically from the start.

data.caption: The iterative writing process with Claude
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A[Define Purpose & Audience] --> B[Request Outline]
  B --> C[Review & Refine Structure]
  C --> D[Request Full Draft]

  E --> F{Good Enough?}
  F -->|No| E
  F -->|Yes| G[Final Polish]

data.title: Watch out for these:
items: Vague prompts that give Claude no audience or format guidance
Accepting the first draft without iteration
Letting Claude make up statistics or facts — always verify
Losing your own voice — Claude should enhance your writing, not replace it
Forgetting that Claude does not know your proprietary context

data.title: Writing with Claude essentials
points: Always specify the audience, purpose, and format in your prompt
Start with an outline, then build the full draft
Iterate with specific feedback — Claude gets better with each revision
Verify any facts, statistics, or specific claims Claude includes
Claude enhances your writing; it does not replace your voice and judgment
